utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning, to everyone. May we take the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Tom Hannis, Gerard Dobbyn, and Sebastiaan van Hooydonk.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Miroslav Cuskic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. We are informed that there is one matter the Defence has before we call the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, just a brief procedural matter. Mr. Zupljanin's Defence submitted on the 30th of September a motion asking to change the manner of testimony of Witness SZ-012 and to have him testify by way of 92 bis. The Prosecution responded to the motion by the Defence, seeking that the whole transcript and exhibits be admitted, specifically two of them that were referred to, 65 ter numbers 20279 and 20280. The Defence would like to inform the Trial Chamber that they have no objection to the admission of these two exhibits. So I think that we can resolve this matter of having this witness testify pursuant to 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So noted. Thank you, Mr. Krgovic. So could the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, good morning to you, sir. Before I invite Mr. Hannis to resume his cross-examination, I remind you, you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. When we left off yesterday afternoon --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- when we left off yesterday afternoon I think you and I were both a little tired but we were trying to go through that list. It's Exhibit P790 at tab 57 in the Prosecution binder. Did you have a chance to look at that overnight and if so were you able to tell us now whether any of the people listed among the 41 who did not sign the new solemn declaration, did any of them continue to work in Prijedor SJB?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did read it. I did read the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, first of all, let me ask it this way. How many of those 41 names of those who did not sign did you know?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't count, but if you like I can go over all of them and tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's not so important how many you know. I guess the question I want to know is -- because --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 40 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. What I'm trying to understand is: It's my understanding that none of them continued to work, they all left. And if I'm wrong about that, tell me who stayed.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the date, the 29th of May, that's the day before the attack on Prijedor. That's when the big mess happened so I don't know where some of the Serbs were either. Perhaps I did meet some of them, but I don't remember who I met and where.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But my question is: After the 29th of May or the 30th of May, are any of those 41 people still working in June and July, August of 1992? They were all gone, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. The station is physically -- is actually quite far away from me, work-wise. Not physically, but as far as work is concerned, it's quite remote. I don't -- I didn't co-operate with those people so I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on to another document then, if we could look at P377. This is at tab 52. And I can give you a hard copy of this one. I'll exchange it for that other one, if I may. Thank you. Now, Mr. Jankovic, this is what appears to be a telegram dated the 28th of May, 1992, from Chief Zupljanin to all SJB chiefs. And he's saying, basically informing, that all employees who did not sign the solemn declaration are dismissed as of the 15th of April, 1992. Did you know about this? Did you see this? What can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall it from that time. I perhaps did see it when somebody from the OTP showed it to me or from the Defence. I don't remember. But I do recall seeing it recently. I don't recall it from that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple questions just about the handwriting on this document. At the top where we see number 11-12/458 and the date, I think that's probably the handwriting of Mira Topic; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. At the bottom there's some handwriting which my English translation records as saying: "The Chief decided that employment is terminated as of 1 April 1992." And a signature I guess. Do you know whose writing that is?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a long time ago but it's familiar. I think and I'm certain of it 80 per cent that this is Milutin Cadjo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was he? Where did he work? What was his job?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the power take-over, he was the reserve -- not reserve, I'm sorry, I made a mistake. He was a retired policeman. After the take-over he was the komandir of the police that was located in our building, it was Prijedor 2 and so on and so forth, Omarska, Ljubija, and so on. He was in the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just some additional explanation. I cannot tell you the official date that he became the komandir because he was putting himself forward right at the beginning and then later he did receive the decision. I don't know exactly the date that he assumed his duties, but he was at that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Assuming that's correct, can you tell us if he's the one who wrote that then who is the chief that he's referring to? Would that be Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a difficult question who he was referring to. I mean, I can just make an assumption that that would be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, that's fine. Okay. That's all I had to ask you about that one. Now, you told us about the 9th of April meeting, and then we know what happened on the 29th and 30th of April. And I think you at some point said between the 9th and 29th during those 20 days you said at page 24774 is that there were obviously some processes, something -- things were going on during those three weeks. I wanted to ask you -- yeah, I want to ask you about a couple of things that appear to be going on. And first of all I want to show you document P354 which I need to find the right page number. It's tab 12 and I'll give you a hard copy of this one. As that's coming to you, sir, I'll tell you that this is a document that's dated the 10th of April. And it's a dispatch from Delimustafic, the minister of the BH MUP to all CSBs and all SJBs. And he's referring to what he called the forcible formation of organisational units in the so-called Serbian MUP being in progress and talking about in his view workers being pressured or blackmailed to sign some declarations of loyalty. He goes on to say that this is -- the activities of the Serbian MUP are illegitimate and that workers aren't required to sign those things. Did you see this? Because based on the number handwritten on the top right, it appears this is a document that was received in Prijedor. I'm sorry, what I've got on the screen is --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Different dispatch is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I've called the wrong number. I wanted to look first at 1D138. I've got my numbers reversed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, witness. The one you're looking at in your hand is from Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is it tab 12 all right, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's tab 12 in my binder. It's 1D138.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know if I just crossed my numbers or not. My apologies to the court officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, did you see this one or did you know about this back in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The way it looks, I believe that it did pass through my communications centre, but unnoticed by me because it wasn't important and the operator didn't inform me and neither did the chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And the handwriting in the upper right-hand corner, again that appears to be the handwriting of Mira Topic, the secretary for the chief.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mira, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want like to look at the other one I referred to, P354, which is at tab 13 and I'll give you a hard copy of that one. Thank you. And you'll see this one is also dated the 10th of April, but it's from Stojan Zupljanin. But it makes specific reference to the one you were just looking at from Delimustafic, that MUP dispatch 09/4-382. I'll tell you that's the number of the one you just looked at. And Mr. Zupljanin is denying that anybody's being forced and that everybody's free to sign up with no pressure. And the last thing he says is the dispatch, Delimustafic's dispatch, does not have any legal effect in the territory of the Serb Republic of BiH and is being put out of force. And again this has what appears to be Mira Topic's handwriting in the upper right-hand corner. So I take it this was another one that was received in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see this one or did you know about this one?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see this document either, but in view of that period, April 1992, and what I said that Chief Talundzic did not, as was customary in earlier times, summon a collegium and interpret the instructions from the top, from the centre. This time he didn't call us chiefs, so I didn't know about it because of that. But he did go to his people. I said that a few times, "his people," but he went for consultations where they interpreted that. But there was no collegium. If there was, perhaps it was an inner circle that I was not a part of. Nobody isolated me per se; I just would like to note that, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So I understand that Chief Talundzic didn't call any kind of collegium and have a discussion about this document, but did you hear any --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But did you hear any informal talk about it, like among the employees in your communications department? Because somebody in your section must have seen it; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communications personnel, including me, were already so immune to the information that we were transferring and perhaps I think that an employee of mine or I could have taken a dispatch to the chief which said that they should kill me and we still would have done it. There were too many information -- pieces of information passing through for us to be able to pay attention to each one. It's -- sounds incredible but that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I understand that general practice of communication workers to just be the conduit for transferring information. And I believe you, what you told us before, that generally you would only look at the address and then deliver the mail, basically, without reading contents. Although, in certain exceptional situations sometimes communications workers did read documents; right? They're human beings.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. That's --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one. Most often they would read the things that they were interested in, for example, salary increases or decreases. Nobody read the politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me then show you Exhibit P1616 at tab 19. This -- I'll hand you a hard copy with the assistance of the usher. And I will tell you, this is a document that I doubt that you have seen before because it's the minutes of a crisis -- or minutes of a Municipal Board meeting or Crisis Staff in Prijedor. It's dated the 23rd of April, so this is during that 20-day period we've been talking about. Have you seen that document before?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. If I did see it during the interview with your side or with the Defence, I don't recall that either. Earlier, I definitely did not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to point out a couple things to you. This is apparently President Miskovic is running the meeting. Mr. Drljaca is one of the attendees at this meeting. And if you would look at number 5 on the decisions that they adopted, number 5 says: "To immediately start working on the take-over, the co-ordination with the JNA notwithstanding." See, I think this is an example of some of the processes that were going on between the 9th and the 29th of April, but I take it from what you've told us before you didn't know anything about that; right? You didn't know anything about the SDS working on preparations for take-over; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I didn't know anything. As I said already, I had nothing to do with the SDS. This Simo Drljaca and the date of the 23rd of April is something I saw for the first time on the 29th of April. In other words, I didn't know him before then, so he was unable to convey anything to me or any police employees unless it was through private channels but not officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That -- fine. I understand that. But with that then I do want to go now and talk a little bit about the 29th of April and the 30th of April. You testified on Tuesday this week you mentioned that you didn't have any previous knowledge about the meeting that occurred on the 29th. You'd been out working in the field on that day and then I think you said --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said at page 24777 you came back around 2.00 in the afternoon and found out -- and found out about the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's the first time you knew there was going to be a meeting that day?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I arrived back from the field, someone called on the phone saying that all people from the communications department ought to attend a meeting. We were notified by phone. It wasn't done in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you said the entire active and reserve police force were invited. Were they also all invited on short notice?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't bother to check, although I suppose as much. The communications department alone would not be left out or not included.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You went on to tell us that when the meeting started there was only one item on the agenda, which was whether or not Prijedor should continue to belong to Banja Luka or should it join Sarajevo. Is that right? That was the topic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there any written agenda or was this only announced orally once everybody was gathered together?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The latter. It was done orally only. No one read out anything. The presiding, the chief of station, Hasan Talundzic introduced the meeting and announced the agenda, the topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take it you didn't take any notes of this meeting like you did of the 9th of April meeting, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I arrived among the last people. I had nowhere to sit down. I was standing, as I said in my statement, next to a pillar like this. I leaned against it and I was unable to write.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that during the meeting you got word that one of your communications officers wanted to talk to you because of a problem he was having sending something; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the name of that communication officer? It's recorded as Dusko --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said already Sarac, S-a-r-a-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to confirm the spelling. And you said you went to see him, he showed you a dispatch -- a coded dispatch received from Sarajevo with an address that required him to send it on to Sanski Most and Novi and Dubica. But he was unable to, you said, because Banja Luka communications officer refused to connect him. Can you explain that technology for me. Why did you and Prijedor need Banja Luka to connect you to your three sort of subordinate stations in terms of communications? I didn't understand that Banja Luka had to be involved when you were communicating with Sanski Most, Novi and Dubica. Is it because this was a coded communication? Can you explain, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you recall, when the two of us discussed the schematic of yesterday, I will remind you that there were two types of communication between Prijedor and Sanski Most. One was a direct line and then a document could be transmitted with a code. The other type of connection was by way of circulars. If they wanted to use the circular communication, then one had to go through Banja Luka because only they had the equipment; if not, then the work you had to do tripled because you would have to take one code, the next code, and the third code, because every participant had its own, whereas in circular communication there was only one. I hope you understand me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think so. And part of this was because it was a coded communication; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But if Banja Luka -- if Banja Luka's communication officer was refusing to make the connection, you could have done it yourself from Prijedor. It just would have taken longer because you would have had to have three separate communications?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know -- do you know who the communication officer in Banja Luka was who was refusing to connect you for purposes of sending this on? Was that Rakovic, the chief?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he's ignorant of it. Not Rakovic, definitely not. He doesn't do that work. It must have been one of his employees but I don't know who. Dusko Sarac was a lazy person, that's why he refused to patch him through. All the rest is excluded. The one in Banja Luka based on his own previous experience of the month before or so -- well, they knew, although I barely noticed it at the time, that some dispatches from the then-republican SUP in Sarajevo in terms of content were such that they were not supposed to arrive at the stations where the SDS was in power with their own cadre. It was because of that that Banja Luka, although the document says "distribute to all CSBs and CJBs," but there was this written or unwritten rule up there that they circumvented them. I realised that there were some such dispatches addressed to Banja Luka which arrived to us and the signalsman in question must have noticed that and that's what he did. If I may add anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction for the transcript. Page 13, line 19 -- 18 and 19. It says that the dispatches were addressed to Banja Luka but arrived to us, whereas the witness said something else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you said about that.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat. A dispatch reads "to all CJBs and CSBs." That means it includes Banja Luka. However, some dispatches - and this one obviously ... - how do I know this one circumvented Banja Luka? Because my signalsman said that this colleague of his there refused to patch him in the circular communication and he said, "Why don't you ask those you work for to patch you through?" He rejected him flatly. That's all I know concerning the dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So if I understand that last bit correctly, you're saying the communications worker on duty at the time in Banja Luka told your communications worker in Prijedor, "Why don't you contact your people" or ask those you work for to patch you through, meaning he was referring to, what, Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But again, you told us that the reason that you read this particular dispatch, contrary to your usual communications worker practice of not reading the contents, this time you read the contents to try and figure out how you can solve the problem of passing this on to the three addressees, Sanski Most, Dubica, and Novi. But I don't understand because you told me you had another way to send it on without Banja Luka connecting you. You could have sent three separate messages. So why did you read this one? You understand? It seems to me you could have solved the problem without having to read the contents but you did read the contents. So why was that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, not reading documents was a principle I followed in my work. It would have required reading an enormous amount of dispatches and this would be a great burden. I had previously --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, let me stop you there because I think I understand what you're saying, but your answer was recorded as: "First of all, not reading documents" -- oh, I'm sorry, it's been changed. So not reading was a principle that you generally followed; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But there was also a regulation in place which stated that an employee of the coding department as well as the officer in charge can read any coded document only to the extent necessary for him to do his job. Whatever he reads is something he may not share with anyone unless the law prescribes otherwise. If this or that document was sent to a particular person, then I can convey information but only to him. That is why being familiar with the situation in terms of communication and knowing that it was a very urgent matter as a rule, dispatches had to leave immediately, at the same moment the signalsman could contact the courier to take it on to the chief because as a matter of principle urgent dispatches concern state matters rather than criminal issues or a fire which had taken place. Since I knew that the chief was there in the meeting and I had to go back, anyway it was only logical that I took the dispatch to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that. Let me ask you, though, about part of your testimony about this. At page 24781 you said even before, whatever the contents of the dispatch, where I saw that it was impossible to apply the standard procedure, I would decide on what measures are to be taken on the basis of contents of the dispatch." I'm not sure I understand what you mean there. What standard procedure are you talking about and why was it impossible to apply?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, if a dispatch arrived in our office and was supposed to go to, say, Bosanski Novi and I know that they cannot receive the dispatch because of technical malfunction, then I'll try to come up with another possibility. If it's an open dispatch, it can be dictated over the phone; if it's a coded dispatch and if so required by the contents -- for example, a dispatch actually arrived saying that this many policemen ought to be provided by Prijedor, Bosanska Dubica, et cetera, to take part in an operation. It was before the war. And I knew that Sanski Most was unable to receive the dispatch, what to do then? You dispatch a courier and a vehicle to take you to them. But I could only propose that and the chief, as a matter of fact, approved. This is what I meant more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On the 29th of April do you know who was in the position of chief of the SJB in Sanski Most, Bosanski Novi, and Bosanska Dubica? Do you know, were those chiefs Serbs or non-Serbs or do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I did know then, but I no longer remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But with regard to this dispatch, given Banja Luka's refusal to make the connection so a circular could be sent, it seems one of the possible solutions as we talked about was to send a separate coded communication to each of the three. But you didn't do that. Was it because it was very urgent and time was of the essence? Is that why you didn't send three separate messages to those three places? Or was it because after you read the contents you decided: Oh, I don't want to send that on. I better tell the chief about it and then we'll decide what to do?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because of the situation in the communications centre and because of what I did when I referred to Prijedor, when I left I no longer came back to control my employee to see what he did what he was supposed to, which was to send it individually to the three addressees. As for the rule that he had to do it, it is so clear he must have known he was supposed to do it and he knew he would bear consequences if he didn't. Concerning the topic of mobilisation, I no longer controlled whether he indeed sent it on, but I am convinced he did, otherwise my work, my job, would have in jeopardy as well. As a matter of fact, no one raised any questions subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand better now. Thank you. So then you took the dispatch to -- well, you took the dispatch and the book to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The dispatch log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have one question about the dispatch. You told us -- we saw the typewritten letters "dzz/m" at the bottom, which you told us you understood to be the -- referring to a communications worker in Sarajevo whose last name was Dzanko; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I think that. I'm positive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I think you said his name was Mirsad. But my information is that communications worker in Sarajevo at that time last name Dzanko his first name was Muhamed. Would you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible too. For example, today I no longer remember the counsel's first name. I've forgotten already. I'm not very good with names, but Dzanko is something I did remember and there were many such work-mates of mine whose initials I was familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You got back to the meeting with dispatch in hand and the book and I think you said you gave it to Mirsad Sahuric to - what? - to fill out in the book the information?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And to give it to the chief and have the chief sign for it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You don't know where that communication book is anymore, do you? Was it destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a book for the chief or by the chief. It could be the one you showed me yesterday. It is only logical. However, I don't remember whether the dispatch is in there. You could check. I think it should be. It should be in his book. As for the communications book where Sahuric made the entry, it's much the same as all the other books.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me see if I understand. So the book the chief signed in acknowledging receiving this dispatch on the 29th of April was the book that Mira Topic kept in the chief's office. Would that be the one you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The official book according to the regulations was the communications book, and it not only included the chief's dispatch but all the other, including the one signed by Mirsad Sahuric. The auxiliary book, so to say, that Mira kept, which I saw yesterday or the day before, I expect you could find it there. I said that the books were destroyed. And I have another remark about destroying books. It wasn't as if we burned a single book at a time. Every month or every week -- actually, every week we would have a full sack of such books to be burned. And when it was this book's turn, it went in the sack as well. Two coding department workers did that. They would take the sack and burn it in a safe place, and it was always done by two people, not a single person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We did look at one book recording I think coded telegrams outgoing. I have another book that I'll show you later on that appears to be incoming dispatches of all kinds that went to the chief. But for now I wanted to ask you, you said the reason that you spoke out at the meeting on the 29th was because of the nature of what you read in the dispatch made you feel as though this was the beginning of a war. Is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you sum up everything I said, it boils down to that, yes. I think I said yesterday too that the answer to your question would be yes. I also said that I started relying on my emotions rather than my senses, and the only thing I felt was this hellish fear of having to face some earlier bad things that had taken place. Before that, I never used to reason that way. I always relied on my rationality alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The reason I ask you about that, I know you told us that you didn't really watch television or read the newspapers, but I wonder were you aware -- well, were you -- first of all, were you aware of the existence of the Autonomous Region of the Krajina and the Crisis Staff of the ARK in Banja Luka? Did you know about that political body that was operating and doing things in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that I did not follow politics, but I wasn't isolated from the world either. I knew that this SAO Krajina existed. As for any Crisis Staff in Banja Luka, I was truly ignorant of that and this is the first I hear of it from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You didn't see any references to the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff decisions, for example, in some of the dispatches received from Banja Luka? Maybe we'll look at a couple later on, but there's some forwarded to Prijedor making reference to ARK Crisis Staff decisions. You don't recall seeing anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you showed it to me, I might be able to tell you something. Otherwise, I don't recall anything off-the-cuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll maybe come to that later. I wanted to stick to my line of questions for right now. So did you not know or hear about a decision by the ARK Crisis Staff on the 27th of April where the -- I'm sorry, it's not the Crisis Staff but it's the Assembly for this point, the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of the Krajina on the 27th had taken the view that the JNA was to be prevented at any cost from withdrawing the equipment and ordnance from the area of the autonomous region. I take it you didn't know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the time, but I did see a document in the papers I received from either you or Defence. I saw it, say, a month or two ago, but I don't recall it from back then. Just another thing. I think you said "Crisis Staff" the first time around and the next time around you said "Assembly." That I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're right, I did initially mention "Crisis Staff." But that particular position was by the Assembly. In late April -- well, in April of 1992, had you heard anything about a group of armed Serbs in Banja Luka that called themselves the Serbian Defence Forces, the S-O-S, did you know anything about them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I assume you didn't hear anything about them blockading the JNA from leaving Banja Luka, starting the 27th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have the feeling that I'm hearing this from you for the first time, but perhaps I did hear about it earlier but it was so important that I completely forgot about it. So perhaps I did hear about it, perhaps I didn't. I mean, Banja Luka was so far away in a sense from us that I never heard it. There was no need for me to hear it. And let me correct myself, I did have a TV set then, but I very rarely watched the news and I don't know if this ever was in the news.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, could I just ask you to clarify a bit. What did you make of the information that you did receive and which you did remember that the Assembly of the ARK had issued a dispatch with the purpose of trying to prevent the JNA from pulling out along with its weapons? What was your interpretation of that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand you properly. You said the Assembly. Are you talking about the Assembly of the Krajina because that was not in the dispatch? If you're thinking about the dispatch that I brought, then that was on the basis of a decision of the Presidency of the BiH, not of the Krajina. That's what I meant. If that's what you meant. I don't know. Could you please clarify your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I can. And I'm glad that I put the question because apparently there is perhaps a misunderstanding. From the transcript of your testimony just a couple of minutes ago, it would appear that you remember having seen the dispatch that was issued by the ARK Assembly --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, if that's in there I don't remember asking a question because the document that I was relying on didn't refer to a dispatch, but it referred to a decision or a position taken by the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. In any case, the way I interpreted your answer, Mr. Jankovic, was that you actually heard of the decision taken by the ARK Assembly on the 27th of April and that this decision was designed to try and prevent the JNA from pulling out its weapons from the Banja Luka area. And my question to you is: Since you seem to remember this decision, what did you make of it? How did you understand the purpose of this decision? Why should the JNA be prevented from pulling out its weapons? Do you understand my question now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do understand it now and I think there is a misunderstanding that originates from what the Prosecutor and I were saying. So I'm going to try to be as clear and as brief as possible. All that I said about the isolation and everything, it all refers exclusively to the dispatch of the BiH Presidency which I brought to that meeting. This was the only thing that I knew. All the other dispatches, documents, that are mentioned in any way, including the ones from the SAO Krajina, I don't know anything about that nor did I ever know. Was I clear? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Jankovic, let me then put the direct question to you. Did you hear at the time of a decision, not a dispatch but a decision, taken by the ARK Assembly on the 27th of April, 1992, a decision to try and prevent the JNA from pulling out along with its weapons from the Banja Luka area? Did you hear of that decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear anything. That's still the period when Talundzic was the chief and if any document did come to the station, as I said a number of times, I was totally "isolated" there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall -- well, let's have a look. I have a technical question for you. Could we bring up Exhibit 1D150, tab 24 of the Prosecution binder. And actually, I know there are two B/C/S versions. It doesn't matter which one we look at first because I want to look at both. Can you see that one on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really see this very well. Perhaps you have a better copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's not much better, but I do have hard copies. If I can hand them to you, I'll hand you copies of both B/C/S versions we have for this. The copy you're going to get may not be much better, but the first point I want to ask you about is: I recall, perhaps in your OTP interview, you explained about the technical functioning of the equipment when sending or receiving these kinds of messages. And there's a unique function of that regarding how the text is oriented on the page if you follow me. I understood if the letters are straight up and down that tells you something about where this one came from, whether it was a sent document or a received document. Do you follow me? Do you know what I'm talking about? And if the letters leaned to the right, that means something else; and if they leaned to the left, that means a third thing. Can you explain that to us? I'm looking at the one that's on the screen now and that seems to be attached -- looking at the one that's on the screen now, that appears to be text that is upright, standing straight up and down. So what does that say to you about where this one came from? That's -- I think that's the one you were looking at in the hard copy. If the letters are upright, what does that tell you about where this came from?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will explain. First of all, based on my experience, I recognise the device on which this was done. This is a teleprinter produced by the Elektronska Industrija Nis factory. And the licence is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So these letters are made up of dots. You cannot see it here but the letters are made up of dots.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The interpreters did not hear the licence. Could the witness please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sagem, yes, that's the French company. Perhaps you know it. They also make mobile phones. That machine has the option of differentiating -- I'm going to tell you now. When the operator is working on the machine, typing on the machine, and the letters are being written, then there is one regime of operation. Can you hear me? When it's being received, when he's communicating with a participant and is receiving the text and directly typing it, that's a second regime. And the third one is when you are making a copy from memorised recorded data. So this particular format indicates that this arrived from a communications line. Recently I did see a document with a copy leaning to the right, recently when I was working with the Defence I saw a dispatch which according to what I know was not a copy but was leaning to the left. So it means that I've forgotten a little bit, but right now I am convinced that the dispatches that were received are straight. And so this dispatch, I think, would have been received directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If in e-court could we put up the other B/C/S version of 1D150 side by side with the one that's currently on the screen. I'd like to have both B/C/S versions up and not the English because I'm just trying to compare the orientation of the text. You see on the screen those two documents and the two documents in your hand. To me it seems -- we've got two copies of the same thing on the monitor. Now, yeah. It seems to me that the darker hard copy, those letters seem to be slanting slightly to the right; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and this is now confusing me. This is opposite to what I have just told you and I don't have an explanation. Why is it opposite? By logic because this dispatch was recorded into the book by Mira Topic, then it would be logical that the dispatch that the chief received, he would hand it over for her to record in the log-book and that it arrived directly, it was received directly. That was the usual thing in the way we worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the dispatch that would be a copy should be slanted. So something is not quite clear to me right now. I don't know how we could get to the bottom of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Don't give up yet. I think you may be right still. You see the handwriting at the top of that one you're holding in your hand which is the one on the right side of the monitor as we're looking at it has the handwriting of Mira Topic; right? Right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it's dated the 11th -- I think it's the 11th of May, 1992, that she's written there; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just remind you of what I said yesterday or the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I'm going to ask you because I think that's correct. You told us that, after the take-over, Mr. Drljaca called you into his office and introduced you to a couple of journalists?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And asked you whether you still had the dispatch?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you went back to your workers to look to try to find the tape whether it was still there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you made a copy?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps that's what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that's why the letters lean to the right on this one; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very probable, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But that would indicate that this one is not the original that Chief Talundzic had because his should have been oriented otherwise, standing upright, not leaning to the right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. From what I can remember on the actual device, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you. That clears up one mystery for me. Now, I want to go on into the evening of the 29th. You told us how after all this happened at the meeting and the hubbub you went home and later on you were called by, I think, your communications officer who was on duty and told to come in. So you went to the police station and when you got there you were told to go to Cirkin Polje; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cirkin Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And who told you to go there? When you got to the police station who told you to go to C. Polje?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just recalling this. I said that yesterday or the day before. The system to summon me when I was needed by anyone, a superior or anybody who really needed me officially, nobody would ever call me at home. They would call the duty officer at the communications centre who was there from 00.00 to 24.00 hours and they would just say: Call the boss to report at such and such a place. And that's how it was this time. I didn't ask him who told him that, but I was summoned to the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, I understand that. But my question is: When you got there then somebody must have told you to go to Cirkin Polje. Who told you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty communications officers were already there and I could see that everybody was getting ready to go, not just the communications staff but the police and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, but can you tell me the name of the person who once you got to the police station told you: We're going to Cirkin Polje? Was that somebody else in communications? Was that the deputy commander of the station? Who do you remember first hearing that you were going to Cirkin Polje?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, most probably the situation proceeded in this way. The person who sent the duty officer didn't say: Call the boss. But he said: You should all assemble. So that when I got there there was some other communications personnel there. It wasn't just me. There were perhaps three of them. I cannot remember who else was there. Raus, Mladen, was there, Milan Batajnica, I don't know if anybody was missing. There were four or five of us. And then there was an assembly already of people there. The communications people were already there. We didn't wait for anybody else. They were all living much closer than I was to the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you told us before about when you got there and the number of people and the kinds of uniforms they were wearing. Do you recall what building specifically you went into? Had you ever been out there before to know what building it was that you were in?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd never been there before. This was a building of the local commune, as we referred to it, over there. This is the place where the secretary of the local commune is. It's a low building about the size of this whole area here, but there are many rooms in that building. I entered an office where there were people whom I knew, perhaps the komandir or I don't recall who it was. In any case, familiar faces. I think that it probably was the office of the secretary himself, that was his place of work. I don't know. There were two or three offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if I understand correctly, this was the very first time that you met Simo Drljaca; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was it from him that you learned that he was the chief from now on? Did he tell you that at that first meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He didn't tell Milos alone. We were just sitting and chatting at the desk, the komandir, all of these were leading officers of the station. I don't remember their names, but I saw them in the days after that. I don't believe that they were all there but many of them were there. And we were just chatting, nothing in particular. There was no panic, then Simo comes in a multi-coloured uniform, I remember the face, tall, he sat. Hello, hello. I'm Simo Drljaca, such and such a thing. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said he was in a multi-coloured uniform. You mean camouflage?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Blue camouflage, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the blue one came into fashion much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I take it you're saying you think it was green on the 29th of April, the one --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military one, green/brown/grey, not blue, a little bit more or a little bit less blue, no, not that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And when he asked you who you were, you told him you were a communications officer and then he gave you, you said, a piece of cardboard that said "official ID" on it; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see you nod your head, but you have to answer out loud for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if you didn't say it correctly or it wasn't translated correctly. Piece of cardboard, no. It was a stack of cards this thick and it said "official ID" and that was something that was to be filled in by hand. And let me just tell you, I remember it was typed in a local printer shop. There were some small letters which said "vila" which indicated to me that it did not come from anywhere outside. Had it come from Banja Luka, the name of the printer would have been one of theirs. So it was obvious that it was printed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. It's time for our first break and we'll follow on from that after we return. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we would resume at 10.45.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, you were just telling us about being handed a stack of blank official ID cards I think you called them. In terms of size, were they about the size of --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what was written on them. It was paper that was much lower quality than what you have, but it was the kind of paper you would use for cigarette packages, but it was the size that you are showing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, I was just showing the witness my ICTY badge. It wasn't on my list of exhibits, but I trust there's no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, did this say anything on it other than "official ID"? Did it say "SJB Prijedor" or "MUP," or did it just have the words "official ID" and then you filled in a name? Was there any other information on these cards? Did you hear my question?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was that side, but it was a bit like this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The procedural issue is that what is now being shown to the witness is something that's not on the record and unless the parties have some violent objection, we propose to have it assigned an exhibit number at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't trying to enter myself into posterity, but I thought perhaps with the agreement of the parties or the Trial Chamber that we can take judicial notice of the size of the ICTY badges that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No, no, not that, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, okay. Good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The documents on the screen are already part of Exhibit 1D150.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: This is the document where there was this difference of views as to the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, but I understood both were attached to 1D150 in e-court --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If I may assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The second B/C/S translation the counsel is using is not entered in the exhibit list yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I thought we'd had a proposal at one time to give it a number of 150.1 or .01.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The second version uploaded by the Prosecution will be assigned Exhibit Number 1D150.1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, I'm sorry about that. Do you recall my question or should I re-ask it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I remember it and I was going to say that is the size but it was double, it was folded over, and "official identification" was written on that -- on the front. Inside something else was written. But as far as I can remember, it did not say "MUP" or "Banja Luka" anywhere. Most probably it said "Prijedor public security station," something like that. And I have a copy, my copy, in my own personal archive. So if necessary, I can provide that. 99 per cent -- well, there was very little text of any kind. There were just lines for the first and last name. There was no post, space for that; there was no space for a photograph or the year of birth of the person to whom it belonged.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take this -- I take it that this was only intended to be used as a temporary document for the purposes of what was happening on the next morning; is that right? This didn't continue to be your official ID at Prijedor after that day; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was used for a long time. It was quite worn from being carried in my pocket. I don't know for how long, but it was months, perhaps longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you filled it out, you put in the names of people as they came up?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did -- what information was filled in on the card other than just the name, any other information? Did you sign on the card as the issuing --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just the first and the last name. Just the first and the last name, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And neither you nor Mr. Drljaca or anybody else from Prijedor signed as the issuing officer, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I definitely did not. I think that there was a small stamp, but it seems that there was no signature. I really can't remember that, but perhaps there was a very small stamp. I don't remember whether there was a signature or not -- his signature. Mine definitely wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If after you're done testifying when you go home, could you have a look and see if you still have yours; and if so, would you be willing to furnish it to us to make a copy of and we'll return the original to you? Are you willing to do that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. Perhaps your staff member can call me on the phone and then we can make some sort of arrangement. I do have an e-mail address. I don't know it off by heart. I can send him a copy by e-mail if that is acceptable to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you're willing to do that, I would ask the Judges to direct the victim/witness people to co-ordinate the logistics with you on that. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't matter to me who would call me. The important thing is for me to know that this is an official thing and that -- and that it's for the needs of this Tribunal. Of course I will do everything else. The important thing for me is to know that it's just not going off somewhere without any control.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... That's why it will be victim/witness, not me or not the other side. It will be somebody who works directly for the Court.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Tribunal, the OTP, the Defence, that is really not in dispute. That will all be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as you know, were you the only person who was filling out those cards and giving them to people that night or did somebody else help you do that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only me that evening. Later on I returned whatever forms were left to the secretary. Later on others received it, but I was no longer familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you keep a list of the names of people to whom you had given cards or did you simply fill out the card and give it to them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This is how it was. Say you arrived, you say your name was this and that, and I write it down. Then the next person came, et cetera. There was no other type of control. Even the people I didn't know personally were included.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that's my next question. So you gave cards -- you gave official cards -- official ID cards to some people that you didn't know who they were; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. But whoever was there I supposed were all -- I don't know. I didn't then -- well, I was -- I did what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you didn't ask anybody to show you an ID that they were a policeman before you gave them one of those official ID cards?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I take it several of the people to whom you gave cards were people that you already knew and worked with as police persons; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You said something that I thought was percipient of yourself. You said that when you were thinking about this you said at page 24798: "So I was asking myself: How come I know nothing about that, whereas there were obviously huge preparations made ahead of it." And I understood you were talking about all these people gathered out there and the take-over being done the next day. Is that right? I mean, it seems the type of thing that must have been planned farther in advance than just the 12 or 13 hours since the meeting where the dispatch was read out. Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I remember I mentioned that I was surprised, but can you tell me more about the context in which I provided that statement? I think I did say that yesterday, but what was the actual context? Perhaps you can expand a bit more or read out a larger portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, the question to you was about the meeting in Cirkin Polje and where it was and where the rooms where. And you said: [As read] "It's a big facility. There are many rooms inside. There was one officer where I sat, but since" --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... "lighting was bad quite a few of them were lit only if you had moonlight. So I was asking myself how come I know nothing about it." And I took that to mean how come you didn't know anything about it before the night of the 29th about all this. That is what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said and that is what I meant. Now I know what you mean. For example, in passing I saw some crates or boxes in a room and they were of the military olive-drab colour. It must have been military equipment. I didn't what it was, where it had come from, who brought it in, and why. It must mean that this was an ongoing process I was unaware of. Of course as a signalsman I wasn't in any situation to know and it's obvious I didn't. Sometimes I learned of things indirectly. For example, before I used to attend collegium meetings when the chief agreed on certain things with the commanders and I was there as an observer and I didn't contribute. But, for example, in this situation I was completely ignorant of the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned at page 24832 when you were asked about what most of the people were wearing at Cirkin Polje, you said there were a motley crew of all sorts of colours, JNA uniforms, then police uniforms that the reserve forces had, the blue ones of poorer quality, there were active-duty policemen in their own uniforms, so everything was there. And then in the transcript I think there's an error you said: "I didn't count, but there were perhaps 1350," 1-3-5-0, "to 200" --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I thought -- did you mean 150 to 200 men?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, approximately. The room was the size of this one and perhaps another half of the courtroom. It wasn't completely packed, but there were a lot of people. I didn't count. Let's put the figure at 150 or between 1- and 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know any of the local JNA commanders in Prijedor at that time? Did you know who any of those were?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did know of them, but I didn't know them personally. For example, Mr. Zeljaja, I had seen him perhaps twice although I didn't see him on that occasion. I'm not saying that he wasn't there, but he wasn't in the same rooms where I was. There were two officers there, though. One was a major and asked for my radio, hand-held radio, Motorola. I had never seen him before. I didn't give it to him because per establishment the military was not part of my structure and I didn't have enough hand-held devices for my own people, let alone the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you recognise any of the people that were in military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't recognise anyone, but at that time or just before there was fighting in Slavonia where the JNA had participated. There were people from our area who went there who kept their relatively worn out military uniforms. There were not police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the number 150 to 200 that you told me about, is that the total number of people in the room where you were?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. We have to be clear. I meant the area around the house. In the house itself there were -- there was a number of smaller rooms and there were far fewer people inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many official ID cards you handed out that night? Was it 50? A hundred? More than a hundred?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall. But that was the only thing I did, although I wasn't at that task all the time. When someone turned to me, I wrote out the IDs. Then there may have been people who didn't even know they would have to come to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now I want to turn to another topic unless the Judges have any questions about that night. Let me show you Exhibit P652. This is at tab 29. I think you may be able to read this one on the screen. Can you see that okay?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a dispatch number 11-12 and there's a handwritten number 1873 at the top. It appears to be from Chief -- from Chief Drljaca to Banja Luka, reporting, among other things, that: "In accordance with the conclusions of the Executive Board of the Serbian Assembly of Prijedor at 0400 hours in the municipality control was seized over SJB and all other major facilities." That is right, that is what happened on the 30 of April?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Handwritten at the bottom we see the date 30 April and 0720 hours, Dragan. Do you know whose writing that is? Is that a communications officer?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. The number of 1.587 seems enormous. I'm not trying to say something there wasn't, but it just sounds out of place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And now about the note. In all dispatches where you come across a handwritten note, it means the following. This is a textbook example and if you remember you can apply it to all other such documents. Each communications worker had their own sign. In the circle it reads BM, Milan Batinica. I was his boss in Prijedor. He sent it. Once he did, the equipment types out who received it. So it was received on the 30th of April, 1992, at 7.20 by Dragan, a signalsman in Banja Luka. It was sent to the CSB there. I don't know this person, but I know that there was a Dragan there. It was standard practice. The person sending it would hand-write their initials. It was much like the DZM on the other document. As for the date, it should be the date when it was sent to Banja Luka and received by Dragan there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Can we go to another topic. I want to ask you what you know, if anything, about some crimes that may have been committed in Prijedor municipality after the take-over. And the first document I want to look at is P659, tab 66. I can give you a hard copy of this one with the usher's assistance. While it's on its way to you, I will tell you this is a -- appears to be a document from Chief Drljaca sent to CSB Banja Luka and dated the 13th of June. And he's complaining about some of the activities of the Banja Luka special unit. Have you had a chance to read that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me know when you're done.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Among other things he's complaining that these special unit people were arbitrarily arresting, interrogating, and abusing prisoners and taking money and jewellery from them and they even got into a conflict with the Prijedor policemen who were on security duty. Did you hear about that at the time, back in 1992, problems with the Prijedor special -- with the Banja Luka special unit in connection with Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear about that. It was so far removed from my tasks that I didn't even know of this "Strazivuk". I don't recall such a last name. I'm not saying they weren't there but I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the last paragraph there's a reference there to Mirko Jesic. Do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the chief of the State Security Service office in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. All right. The other item is he mentions that there were also complaints about the conduct of the special unit and looting during mopping-up operations. Was that referring to operations in the Muslim villages in Prijedor municipality that was done in May and June of 1992? What did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what is referred to specifically in the document, but I believe there were such incidents. There was chaos and I could see it for myself. I was stopped once by someone. They weren't police, and they wanted to take away my vehicle. It was an official Golf vehicle. They were trying to seize it in the name of the people they said. I did scare them away when I said I was a policeman, but they simply wanted to take the car away. I believe there were such instances. As for what was official, unofficial, or semi-official is difficult to discuss from this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't think you mentioned this incident before. When and where did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. I didn't mention it. I was reminded by what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was on official business to the radio station in Prijedor. It had something to do with communications. I don't remember exactly. There was a person with an old olive-drab coat and an old rifle and he said, "Hand-over the keys in the name of the people."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a silly elderly guy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let me show you Exhibit P812. It's at tab 111 of the Prosecution binder. And I'll hand you a hard copy, although it's not very good either. It appears --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh my.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, it appears to be to the Prijedor SJB from CSB Banja Luka, forwarding a telegram from Minister Stanisic, wherein he orders that an investigation be done into the fate of about 150 Muslims who apparently were killed in the area of Skender Vakuf at Koricanske Stijene. Did you ever hear about that event?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, but much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the circumstances under which you first heard about it, when and where and how you heard about it for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall very little. Brane or Branko Siljeg was an inspector in charge of property crimes and crimes related to economics. It's the person I mentioned in relation to the medication in Keraterm. By that time he was a ruined person, ruined by alcohol. He told me he went there with someone - he never said who - and he didn't even tell me the whole story. He just said, "We went," and he said, "I'm tired because I went beyond Knezevo" and that some people were killed and I guess they were there to clean up and that's why they went there. But at the time it didn't mean much to me. The topic of death was an everyday thing at the time. And I also didn't take his information seriously, having in mind what kind of person he was. He died later on because he had drunk too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on when I worked in the CSB in Banja Luka, they commemorated it, it seems. After the war when I moved following 2001, I think Bosniaks commemorated the event; and we provided security, the police. We from the communications department didn't attend the scene itself, but we were around the perimeter, say almost a kilometre away. I was never on the spot. I simply took part in preparing the communications side of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So in 1992 did you hear anything else about this event at the Koricanske Stijene being discussed in Prijedor police department, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No one discussed it. The first news came from this colleague. As I said, he said he was tired because he had been there. I have a feeling it was 15 or 20 days after the crime, maybe less, 10, but then it could be 30 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're not aware of a number of dispatches back and forth between CSB Banja Luka and Prijedor regarding that event? Do you remember seeing any dispatches about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from that time, but you prompted me or perhaps the Defence - I don't remember who - because your dispatches resemble theirs. It could be one of yours. I may have seen it, and I think I even saw on a dispatch that Simo -- well, I can be disrespectful and tell the -- I think he said: "I didn't conduct an interview because the people were absent." In our service this was not a normal way to go about things. He could have gone out in the field and find them, but I did see it when I read your dispatches, not before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Certainly not in 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one more thing in this context. The dispatch I have in my hand, this one, from the minister, obviously this was not typed out on any communications equipment. Perhaps a typewriter and then it was faxed. If it was received by Banja Luka, I can't even read what it says, but speaking from my experience, if Banja Luka received it from Sarajevo by fax then this is it. I don't think this had gone through the communications centre, any communications centre, including Banja Luka. That's why the copy is so poor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah, let me show you a couple other documents that may shed some light on this. If we can look at Exhibit P1380, it's tab 112. Witness, this one you may be able to read on the screen, it's a better copy. It you need a hard copy, let me know. Can you read that one all right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, this is enough, what's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. This one is dated the 11th of September, 1992, it looks like, from CSB Banja Luka to Prijedor to the chief and it says: "We received the following dispatch numbered 10-245/92 dated 31 August ... from the MUP ..." And then it's from Minister Stanisic ordering you to conduct a full investigation. So it looks like basically the same order that you were looking at on that bad copy just a minute or two ago. And then below the text of Minister Stanisic's order are some specific directions from Mr. Zupljanin to the Prijedor chief. At the top we see handwriting with a number 11-12-668 and a date. Is that again Mira Topic's handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then what appears to be maybe different writing, I'm not sure, the word that has been translated as the name "Marko."

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it as Marko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Do you know what that or who that refers to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
