utterances.text: As far as I know, there was just one Marko, Marko Djenadija, who I already mentioned. So at that time Marko -- well, Marko was a komandir somewhere. Even later after the war he was chief of the station. But right now I don't see any role for Marko. I don't know of any other Marko except Marko Djenadija. I don't know what his role there is either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what position he held in September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just said I cannot remember. For a time during the war, he was the komandir of the station Prijedor 2, I think, or the traffic police because they were outside of the centre building. But from when to when, I really couldn't say. Cadjo, Marko, they all followed one another. So I'm afraid I would make a mistake now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you two other documents relating to this and then I think we'll move on. Exhibit P682, which is tab 113. This is another one I think maybe you can read on the screen. It's dated the 14th of September from Simo Drljaca to CSB Banja Luka, to the chief. And it's -- I think it's a response to the one -- yes, the one that you were just looking at, 11-1/02-2-345. And here he's saying we can't investigate because those policemen that escorted the convoy have been at the battle-field since 9 September. Is this the document you referred to before when you said you thought you'd seen one where Drljaca was saying --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was thinking about him earlier. I don't remember from what period. The first time I saw him, I don't know whether this was in conversation with your people or the defence, but I did see that recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And one more, tab 114. This is 65 ter number 20268. It appears to be a coded dispatch dated the 14th of September from Drljaca to the chief in Banja Luka, again referring to that same dispatch number. It says: "We're not able to conduct an investigation since all the policemen have been deployed on the front since 9 September and also we're unable to provide you a list of the citizens who travelled on those convoys because this public security station didn't organise the convoys but only assigned a certain number of policemen to providing physical security." The Dusko S. and the date of 15 September, tell us about that. Is he a worker in your comms centre?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is not the S, but it's the Sh, Sarac that I mentioned before who had called me about that dispatch. And then again you can apply the logic that I spoke about recently in relation to these handwritten parts, that means the dispatch was handed in, the chief wrote the 14th of September, it was sent on the 15th of September; at a normal time this would be an incredibly long time for it to be sent off to Banja Luka. You see 0750 here. So I'm talking about what we talked about, the difficult operation of the communications system, meaning that it had stayed there all day. Then this guy, Dusko, there's a Dusko up there as well. This Dusko received it from this other Dusko. There are two Duskos, one in Banja Luka and one up here. Received by Dusko at 7.50 and it was dispatched by Dusko Sh, Sarac, that's our guy at our end.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So it was sent and it was received in Banja Luka then according to this?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was received according to what Dusko wrote, at 7.50.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to tender that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would object to this because I believe that this document should not be admitted because the Prosecutor is actually tendering new evidence and in light of fresh evidence this document does not meet that criteria. The Prosecutor did not give a clear reason why the document was not admitted earlier when it admitted the identical document as P00682. And for those reasons, I believe that the document should not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, why would -- why was not this tendered at the time that the Prosecution tendered the - I will call them - companion documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know the answer to that question, but I do know I came across this in preparing for this witness and trying to identify documents that dealt with what I perceived to be the allegation in the 65 ter summary for this witness that Mr. Drljaca was not -- was acting independently and was not responding to requests for information from CSB Banja Luka and Mr. Zupljanin. And that's why it was proposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Apart from that, this is -- seems to be tangential in terms of the witness who is presently on the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, he is able to verify that it was sent and it was received based on his knowledge of how the system works and recognising the handwritten information with the names of two Duskos. I wasn't able to present that evidence through any other witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may reply. The previous document was shown to the communications chief by the Prosecutor. He could have done the same with this document as he had with the previous one. There were several witnesses, actually, in particular the communications chief who discussed it. And that witness was used to introduce a number of documents through by the Prosecution. They had an opportunity to deal with it. A number of other books were tendered through the same witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We will have the document only marked for identification because one of the considerations that we would wish to -- upon which we would wish to reflect is the -- any degree of prejudice that the Defence suffers and how it could be remedied. So for the time being we -- the document is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2394, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, I want to move to another topic. Did you know a police officer in Prijedor named Slobodan Miljus, M-i-l-j-u-s?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard such a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you, did you -- did you know about the disciplinary procedures in the MUP in 1992, how that system worked, what the rules were? Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. Actually, I was familiar with it before the war and I know how things worked when I was in Banja Luka after 2002. Before the war there was a disciplinary commission. The chief in question had to put forth a proposal and then the commission would sit and decide on one's disciplinary liability. After the war in the Banja Luka centre, there was a prosecutor who was there only to deal with cases involving official personnel. Upon receiving a proposal from the commander, the Prosecutor dealt with it by way of an internal court of sorts. It was not a state court. They ruled according to the disciplinary regulations in place. When that -- the transfer occurred between the previous and the new system is something I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. I'll move on to something else then. I'd like to ask you in terms of communication, were you aware of -- I don't know what to call it. Related to the ministry on National Defence or the defence ministry, are you aware of a communications system that sometimes was referred to as the, I don't know, the information and warning system, something like that? Do you know what I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose. You weren't quite precise in your definition, but I think the name was centre for information, reconnaissance, and warning. It was in the municipality, I think. It was used in terms of -- in cases of disasters, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's -- I think you're talking about the thing I was curious about. I want to show you Exhibit P179.9. This is tab 31. I'll just show you the cover page and then take you to a specific paragraph. This document's from May 1992 and it's called "decision on the organisation and work of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality." And if we could go to page 4 in the English and in e-court the B/C/S is page 4. And at the bottom item 8 or Article 8. Can you read that okay, Witness, Article 8? It says: "In order to work effectively within the area of civilian protection and reconnaissance and information service, the Crisis Staff shall do a couple of things and the second one is: "Via the Municipal National Defence Secretariat undertake measures and actions aimed at ensuring the successful functioning of the Communications System and the Reconnaissance and Information service." Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry? Via the municipal staff -- can you repeat again the second item of Article 8. It says I think via the Municipal National Defence Staff and other elements, undertake measures and actions aimed at -- I can't read it. Civil protection, its tasks. I can't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I take it what the interpreters have translated into English is saying that: "Via the Municipal National Defence Secretariat, undertake measures and actions aimed at ensuring the successful functioning of the Communications System and the Reconnaissance and Information Service."

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I understand now what the question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So my question is: Did you know about the existence of that service and its communications system?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. The centre existed before I came to the police. This is a centre that is located in the basement of the municipal building, and they had equipment that used different frequencies from ours and the purpose of that equipment was for natural disasters, floods, and that's why it's called the centre for alerting and informing. So they also have the sirens that you can sometimes hear in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know that that service and its communications system, network, was sometimes used to transmit information from, for example, Pale and the republican-level authorities out to Crisis Staffs and Municipal Assemblies in places like Prijedor and Banja Luka? Did you know about their system working and how it worked during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know much about that centre because I wasn't interested. I had no functional connections with them. It's true that there were some links between our centre and theirs, but I didn't have any particular interest work-wise. But it's true that each municipality in Bosnia and Herzegovina has such a centre or had such a centre. And by size and complexity, this corresponded to the size of the municipality. There was a large centre in a large municipality, a small centre in a small municipality. And organisationally and constructively they were intended to facilitate communications within the municipality between the local commune, and by virtue of that they had local connections and frequencies. I don't know if they had connections that were broader than that or not, and perhaps they could set up communications further out or not. I don't know. I never followed that. I never visited. I never was interested. It wasn't open access, where they worked just like at our centre. It was only for privileged persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mean like the Crisis Staff, privileged persons like the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I know who could enter our premises and who could not. As for them, I don't know. I was never interested. I never asked. I don't know whether the Crisis Staff entered or not. Conditionally speaking, my centre where I was the chief, the only people who could enter would be the operators, the staff, the chief, myself. Nobody else besides those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So in 1992 you never had occasion to ask for assistance of that service in transmitting any documents?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not, no. Because we were more professional than they were I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you just before the break one more document, Exhibit 1D397. And hopefully you can see this on your screen. This is another document related to the 29th of April. This is not the one from Minister Delimustafic, but it's forwarding a document from Colonel or Commander Hasan Efendic. But I'm not so interested in the content. I want to ask you some questions about the delivery information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's tab number 27, Exhibit 1D397.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you see it okay on your screen, Mr. Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see just a bit. It's not complete. The letter-head or the heading is not good and I don't see the signature.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We do not hear what the witness is saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it says up here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You see a five-digit number 41505 and then little letters SO followed by the letters PLE. Do you know what that --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I couldn't see it at the angle that I was sitting at. I have to stand. Yes, I can see it now really well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you want the hard copy so you don't have to stand?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I mean, I can do it like this as well if it's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all right, you can see it really well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the number 45254 SUPBL, do you know what those stand for?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that is for our communications, the police ones, that probably has nothing to do with that. But from what I can remember, and I don't remember that very well, this YU at the end, these are public PTT communications, that this was a dispatch sent through the public system -- maybe, maybe. I think this 4150 would be the public telecomms just like if you were sending a telegram to somebody, congratulations. I think that that's that system; our system didn't have the letters YU.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever hear of something that was called the republican communications centre in the RS in 1992, located in Pale?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I think it's time for our next break, Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Zecevic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note that the translation of this document is incomplete, unfortunately. This is the first time I saw that. Because you will see that after the words: "We are forwarding this ... for SDS BiH ..." there are two lines stating five numbers and then SOSMYU and then, again, five numbers that say Vlada [phoen], Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina YU. So the document needs to be sent to translations in order that the translations are complete of the whole document. And since it is a 1D document, we will do that. I just wanted to put that on the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Zecevic. So we will resume at 12.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before the witness comes back in, the counsel would have been alerted by the Chamber through our Legal Officer about the discoveries in terms of this document that was marked for identification. Do you have anything to -- do you have any observations, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In the light of that discovery, I don't think I have the same problem that I did. I understand P682 is the same document minus the handwritten notations by the two communication officers the witness testified about. So I think, given the fact that I have P682 in evidence, which is the text of the telegram, and I have the testimony of this witness about that, reflecting that apparently it was sent and received based on viewing those two signatures, I don't need it in. I suppose I would prefer to have -- what's been MFI'd as P2394 in evidence instead of 682 because it's a more complete document. That would be my preference. I understand the one with the handwritten notation by the communication officers was disclosed to the Defence back in 2008. Why we used the one without the signatures instead of the one with signatures, I don't know. I think that was probably just a glitch in the selection process. Somebody looked at it, thought it was the same thing, and picked what now I would say was the wrong one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krgovic, there appears to me to be an irresistible logic to what Mr. Hannis is suggesting. We just substitute the incomplete document for the complete one. Do you have a problem with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, it's a problem that's in principle. That's what I was talking about. This is new evidence that pursuant to the instructions of this Trial Chamber should not be admitted. This is a principled objection. The Prosecution had the document, it was on its list, and it did not tender it, and it did not provide a valid reason why they did not do this. And that is why I believe a precedent like this, no matter how logical it might seem, would open the door to the admission of similar documents in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, what would be new about it? You say it's new evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a new version of this document. I don't have a problem with old documents in the record for them to stay in the record, that would be sufficient for me, and the Prosecutor has the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber is satisfied that the document that has been marked for identification should now be entered in substitution for -- thank you, for P682.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And we vacate -- sorry, what was that number again? P2394. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, I now want to turn briefly to a document about Prijedor SJB. This is tab 74 in the binder. It's Exhibit P657 and I think it will work best if I can give you a hard copy because it's several pages. I will tell you as it's coming around, this is a report from Chief Drljaca to Banja Luka and to the -- I guess to Banja Luka at least, June 1992, and it's a report on activities in the first half of 1992. And the first point I want to ask you about is page 2 in e-court in English and B/C/S. And for you, witness, it's that left-hand page on the table in front of you, the bottom paragraph. Yeah. I think just above that paragraph there's a reference to the take-over of power by force which was carried out on 29 April without a single shot being fired. Do you see that? It's above that paragraph about eight lines up. You find the date 29 April.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says: [As read] "The incident of the 29th and beside that extremists from the ranks of the HDZ have totally prepared to take absolute power over and engage in unprecedented terrorism against the Serbian population which necessarily resulted in intensive and continuous preparations for a take-over of power by force which was carried out on the 29th of April without a single shot being fired and without bloodshed."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And two sentences after that it says, "They prevented" -- it's talking about the extremists from other national parties. "They prevented non-Serb SJ employees from signing statements on loyalty." Did you know anything about that about HDZ or SDA extremists keeping non-Serb police employees from signing the new statement of loyalty or solemn declaration as it's sometimes called?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This is too narrow. In the context of what? I don't know if there were any. I don't know. It's -- I'm not aware of them. Perhaps there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's talking now about the taking over of power of the 29th of April and that the extremists prevented that. When? Before or after? When? Nothing is clear to me. And I don't remember any of that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me take you to something that's more in your field. It's page 4 of the English in e-court. And for you, Witness, it's -- well, in e-court it's page 5 of the B/C/S. Yeah. You'll see a section on "work and tasks and maintaining the communications system." I think you've got it there. You see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. That number -- no, I think you're on the correct page because when I say "page 5," it includes the cover page so it's the page number 4, yeah. And that talks about the kind of work that was done to maintain the communications system. So you guys were working not only in Prijedor but were you also helping assist Dubica, Sanski Most, and Novi?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If you could turn to the next page and in e-court we have to go one page further in the B/C/S but stay on the same English. If you could turn to the top of the next page. My English translation says: [As read] "In addition to the above ... activities, a whole number of other individual ones were ... carried out, such as working on power generators and power supply equipment and ... working on the UKT," ultra short-wave equipment, "in war time conditions ..." And the last sentence says: [As read] "It is necessary to mention that during preparations for military operations, four mobile and three fixed radio stations were fixed using obsolete radio stations and given to users." Did you know about that? Did you participate in that activity, providing four mobiles or fixing four mobiles and three fixed radio stations in connection with preparations for military operations?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this here is a little bit. If I understood this last bit just a little bit, because Simo is talking about preparations to avoid any unclear matters. What was done? I was definitely, just like all bosses, producing reports for everything and submitting them to my boss, who was Simo at the time. So I would look at my records and all of this that is written here, how many stations repaired, and so on and so forth. And then that would be done and then I don't remember now but due to a general lack of - how should I put it? - lack of -- well, equipment was deteriorating and then perhaps we would repair old equipment that was out of commission. But it was not something that was part of a preparation for a take-over of power. That was part of our regular work. And if Simo - perhaps I don't see this here, perhaps I'm making assumptions about all of this because I don't see if Simo wrote this or not because he maybe saw that as us doing that in some sort of preparation for his coming, perhaps he saw it like that, but it wasn't like that at all. We were just doing that as part of our regular service. And, yes, here he wrote: "It is necessary to note that during preparations for current military operations ..." you could see that the technical job that was done was correct that I put in a report that was done, and then when I write I don't usually comment this station was nice, this one was good, this one was no good. I just put the numbers there from the staff that was working on them, how much was done, as you can see on the list. And then you can see that Simo was evidently presenting that somewhere further up as if we were doing some sort of something. This was all done as part of our work. The communications centre could not have been working parallel on two tracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you a few questions to clarify. That text that we just read out in this report, I'm operating under the understanding that that was written by Mr. Drljaca, not by you; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. His, not mine. My report perhaps has three pages and then he just takes what he needs, numbers and then he puts his own writing in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm assuming these numbers on the previous page about the types of equipment repaired and all those numbers came from you; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah. But the reason I'm asking you about this reference to preparations for military operations and certain radio equipment in connection with that, is that I can't remember exactly where it was but you were -- you were asked about if you were aware of the Prijedor police being involved in any military operations in the municipality in May and June and you said something along the lines: No, that couldn't be because I would have known about it, because they would have needed my communications support. Do you remember that? Do you remember having a question and answer like that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it hazily. Could you be more specific? What do you have in mind? What operation? I'll try to be clearer. If there is a one-time operation, they can ask for communications assets from me and return them following their operation. Now, whether they did something without asking for my equipment is something I no longer remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I had the impression that you were saying that as far as you knew in May and June of 1992 no police were involved in combat operations in Prijedor municipality because you would have known about it because you would have had to have been involved in communications support. And I took it your answer to mean that all those combat activities in the area of the Muslim villages, Kozarac and Hambarine and Biscani, et cetera, were done by the army with no police. I took that to mean that was what you were saying. Is that what your belief was, that the police didn't anything to do with any of those?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you just said is something I believe I said already. I'm trying to recall it now, but from the fact that I don't know you can't conclude that the police did not participate. I'm simply saying that they did not ask for my assistance. There were always pieces of equipment that were constantly used and then if they needed a surplus, they asked. They could have carried out an operation with such pieces without requiring any additional ones. In any case, if they did anything of the sort, I wasn't included.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That answers my question. If we could go to page 5 of the English in e-court and, Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but I think that this part of witness's response is not properly recorded. Line -- it's page 61, line from 10 until 17. Witness said something different - it's not recorded - about the -- he used the word "vecim operacijama" [Interpretation] larger operations or more important operations. That part is missing. Could we please have it repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, you heard what Mr. Krgovic said. I understood you to be saying that the police may have participated in combat operations without you knowing about it because they may have been able to use radio equipment that they already had or perhaps that they got from somewhere else. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from someone else. They definitely could not receive that. They either had their own or, actually, the ones they were issued with - and I'm the custodian, actually -- however, I only see such pieces of equipment when they break down or when they need to be recharged by my technicians. In any case, I was the boss and in charge of monitoring it all. The police definitely used communication means that they had at their disposal, although I don't know whether these were pieces of equipment that they regularly used or if they needed something on top of that. I don't remember. It could have happened that someone asked for one or two hand-held radios, but it's such a small number that I wouldn't remember it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can go to page 5 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for you, Witness, it's -- in e-court it's the B/C/S page 7. I think for you, Witness, it's page number 6 at the top. Yeah, I think it's that page. And the paragraph that starts under the bullet point that says 14 charges were filed. It says "in the second quarter," do you find that? "In the second quarter, the take-over of power took place ..." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah. "... and fighting broke out. All Muslim and Croatian officers refused to sign statements of loyalty and some even actively participated in the armed rebellion. Activities were focused on covering the terrain, protecting socially owned and private property and participating in combat operations." So from that I understand that some of the Prijedor police were participating in combat during this time-period prior to Mr. Drljaca's report; would you agree? That seems clear.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We need to be precise. Who and in what fighting? Do you mean Muslims or Serbs when you say "some"?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, he's talking about -- the report is about the Prijedor SJB and so he says "... activities were focused on covering the terrain, protecting socially owned and private property and participating in combat operations." I assume he means the Prijedor police were doing that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Keep going.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then it talks about the captured extremists from these combat operations because there were so many three reception centres were established, Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje. My question is about the next sentence. It says: [As read] "All operative officers were engaged in carrying out investigative activities." One question comes to mind. You said your wife worked in the department in economic crimes. To your knowledge was he involved in investigations on Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje? Was she an operative?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she was, but she was also the only female among all operative employees. It was probably for that reason that her boss did not send her to Omarska or Keraterm to work. It was quite tiresome even for men. They needed a person in the centre at all times anyway for some small tasks. There were no interrogations or operative treatments there. They simply needed someone who would be there on duty and it was because she was a woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that answered my question. She didn't have to go to Omarska or Keraterm or Trnopolje in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the rules of service, she should have. But she did not have to thanks to her boss. She wasn't made to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that's all the questions I had for that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As you move on, appreciating that you began with the comparative disadvantage of not having had the opportunity to speak with this witness beforehand, the -- do you think that you would, having now spent some time with him on the stand, do you think you would need all of the two hours and 40 minutes that you have left of what you had required?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My estimate earlier today when somebody asked me I think I will need one session tomorrow. I don't need time beyond the eight hours, but I think I may need my full eight hours. I suppose I might finish in an hour tomorrow. I know I have two particular topics and documents that I want to cover tomorrow that are the most important remaining things and I'll try and do everything else between now and 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, I want to show you now another document regarding Mr. Drljaca. It's tab 30, but before I bring that up, though, let me ask you this: Do you remember when Mr. Drljaca left the Prijedor SJB and took up a position in the office of the Ministry of the Interior? Did you know that? He held a position in I think the office of public information? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he did, but I do know he was replaced. He was no longer in Prijedor but in Bijeljina. I don't know what he did there, though, and he did return later on. He wasn't away too long, but I don't know what he did there. As far as I remember, Bogdan Delic was the station chief in the interim period. It's been quite a long time ago and many people rotated. I think it was Bogdan and I'm sure the other was in Bijeljina, although I don't know what he did there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But in Bijeljina it was with the police, it was a job with the police, with the Ministry of the Interior; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And he returned to be the chief in Prijedor, at least by sometime in 1994, he was again the chief; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did return and again he was the chief. I think it was when I was on sick leave. I did used to see him, but I can't be specific as to the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember when you began your sick leave in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1994 it was definitely sometime in March. I would have to try and recall it all. I was in the hospital for a month and then there was a recovery period of 40 days. There was an operation in June, but all the medical checks they had to do took quite a long time. I think sometime in March, in the spring of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. I think the document I have that reflects him back as chief in Prijedor is from April of 1994, so you may not know about that. And speaking of Mr. Drljaca, you mentioned Tomasica as a place you had to drive by sometimes when you were travelling from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's my understanding there is a mine there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about hundreds or thousands of Muslim bodies having been placed in the Tomasica mine in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How would I know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, it seems like --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One doesn't hear such things, and even if you do you don't want to listen to it. Who killed whom where and what they did with them. If I heard such a thing, I forgot it on the spot. But I'm pretty sure I have never heard this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could look at 65 ter -- no, I'm sorry, tab number 143, Exhibit P1767. And, Witness, I think I need to give you a hard copy of this one. You will not have seen this before I'm sure. I will tell you this is an excerpt from what's been identified as a diary of General Mladic from 1993 and the entry we're looking at is from the 27th of May, 1993, and I would like to go to page 4 of the English and page 4 in the B/C/S in e-court. And this is Colonel -- at the bottom of the fourth page for you it's got that little green stickie on it. Yeah -- no, go back, go back one page. Yeah. The bottom left page you'll see is highlighted in pink. It's Colonel Bogojevic speaking apparently and he says: "4 to 5 days ago Simo Drljaca arrived, the former Chief of Prijedor SUP, sent by the minister of the RS and he came about the Tomasica mine." And you have to go on to the next page in English and B/C/S: " ... near Prijedor, where earlier they had buried around 5.000 Muslims bodies. I'm sure the world knows about this from the released prisoners. "Drljaca came to leave this with us and they want to get rid of it (by burning, grinding, or some other way). "There are all kinds of bodies and they have involved Subotic," who I believe is a reference to the minister of defence Bogdan Subotic. "The team includes Drljaca, he was in charge even while this was being done, at the meeting were General Subotic, Arsic, Drljaca, me, and Mile Matijevic from the BL SUP." So you never heard any rumours about this, about bodies in the Tomasica mine?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I hear about something like this for the first time in my life, about Tomasica. I never came across a number of 5.000 corpses. It's an enormous number. I would have remembered something of that sort. I didn't hear of any much smaller numbers, let alone 5.000. It would involve columns of trucks. I don't believe this. If Simo did, there must have been reasons for it. But as for the entire entry, it's something I have never heard about. The number of 5.000? No way. It must be a hundred times over whatever it could have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, did you ever hear of any smaller number of bodies of Muslims being in the Tomasica mine?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, not in Tomasica but, for example, what we mentioned a moment ago, Koricanske Stijene, and the figure of 50 or 80. I heard about such figures in different situations, but not 5.000. Not in my life. I don't think even in Jasenovac there were as many people killed. I have never heard of Tomasica being mentioned in this context. I know there was a mine there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Next I think I need to go back to one log-book. I think you and I like to do that, but I'm not sure anyone else does. I'd like to hand you tab 128.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was hoping you lost them along the way, but you kept them it seems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you're not the only one that was hoping that. I'm sorry, I do want to show you this one if I may. And I'll have the usher hand you a hard copy. And let me just find the correct starting page for you. This is Exhibit P1025. And can you tell us from the cover page anything about what it is? It simply seems to say "book 91, 92, 93, 94."

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think archaeologists would be better suited. I don't remember this book. Perhaps if I opened it I might be able to see something more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If you could go to the page I've marked, we'll look at some of the documents listed in there and that may help you identify what it is, the yellow tab at the top will take you to 1992. That's page 86, I believe, in e-court in the B/C/S. And it's the first page in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think the witness is having problems with the clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He's got it off now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you see that, "1992"? I believe you were shown this book or parts of this book --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were shown parts of this book during the OTP interview by Mr. Yarmah and Ms. Beausey and you were able to identify some of the handwriting. Now, I'm not so interested in the first part of the year when Mr. Talundzic was the chief. If you could begin by looking at -- well, first, before I take you to the first entry I wanted to ask you about, could you go to the last page for 1992, which as you page through you will see the last entry is numbered 828. So if you're reading the numbers in the left-hand column, can you go until you get to 828, which is 118 in e-court in the B/C/S and the last page of the English.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at the bottom --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. At the bottom we see a -- some writing and a date and what appears to be a signature. Do you recognise any of that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This looks like MT, Mira Topic. But I don't remember her specific signature. I'm also looking at the hand-writing. All things put together it should be her. I think it's her handwriting and the initials could be MT, Mira Topic, but otherwise she didn't use to sign documents much. She was a secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. I think when you looked at this document before you identified some of the handwriting in this as being Mira Topic's, but there was a portion where you indicated that some of the writing appeared to be by some of your communication people. I would like you to look first at page -- or for the entry that is number 300 and --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 302. And that's --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't have said that it was our signalsman. I don't recognise this handwriting --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, right now I just have a question about --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, right now I just have a question about some of the abbreviations. Under the column "from" it says MUP of the SRBHSSR. Do you know what SSR stands for in that context?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: SRBH MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was the official title before the multi-party elections and the new constitution. That was in SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there's a column for urgency and it's column number 6 and then column number 7, system. I think you've explained about some of the designations, but I just want to be clear. The DX, that stands for non-urgent; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not correct. You were rushing along, so I will repeat. O, DD, DX, and B are urgent. The rest are usual dispatches or ordinary ones. DX in terms of context are separate. These are urgent operative measures. If someone stole a bicycle or raped a woman or hit someone with a car and fled, then such information would be included in DX dispatches. The contents defined that type of dispatch and the dead-line was two hours. DD and very urgent, these are state matters, say if there was an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are designations for urgency depending on the type of information they contain. DX, urgent operational measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the -- in the next column we'll see either I think one of three designations, either O, which I understand means open; Sh, which means coded; and very urgent is another designation?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two designations, depending on the urgency and confidentiality. Both contained O's. In the first one it means plain; in the second case it is open. You can have an OO dispatch, which is the lowest on the list in terms of importance. They could take the most time and were of least relevance. A double O would mean plain open. However, they could all be coded and they could all be open. The very urgent dispatches were regularly coded. DX, for example, could be very urgent but open.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you could go to page -- in e-court the B/C/S is page 92 and it has the first entry at the top as number 176, which in e-court the English is page 7. Do you recognise the handwriting on that page, Mr. Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one moment, 199 --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in the same year; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. 176 at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. 176.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you look at that and the following four or five pages and tell me, is that the writing of Mira Topic or someone else?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That first one definitely is not, but I cannot remember who it is. I don't know. I know as much as you do. When you look at the two handwritings, they're not the same, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not as far as I can see. I could be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you would continue on to page 98 in e-court in the B/C/S and go to document number 320 and in English in e-court that's page 13. Do you find that one?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's it, 2266, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's it, that's it. The top five or six entries appear to be by someone else, and from number 332 on, that looks like the writing that we've come to associate with Mira Topic; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what it looks like to me too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from what -- take all the time you need and if you want you can take this home with you at the end of the day. But would you take a look at the nature of the dispatches and in the right-hand column the indications as to who signed for it or for who it went and tell me if you can draw any conclusion about whose book this was, who kept this book, and what it is. Is it incoming documents? Is it outgoing documents? Is it a book that was in your comms centre or was it a book that Mira Topic kept in the chief's office, if you can say based on looking at the documents. And if you want more time, we can set that aside and you can take it home with you when you go home this evening and tell me in the morning or if you think you only need a couple of minutes right now, we can do it right now. I leave it up to you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I leave here so tired, I don't recall when I felt so tired the last time, when I was taking my final exams at school or university. So perhaps we can have an extra ten minutes and we can finish that together with the Prosecutor. So I might have a tendency to go off on a tangent and perhaps if we go through this by talking, point by point, then I can deal with that. Otherwise, I have to worry about if I take the document, where would I take it, what would I do with it. Perhaps then we can just have your permission to stay just ten minutes longer and just complete this right here. I mean, if I have to, I will take it with me. I would put it somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. The reason I ask was maybe I should go back and look at your OTP interview because I know it was shown to you and talked about with you and maybe if I can point you to some parts of that interview that will refresh you memory. That might be a more efficient way to do that. I can do that in the morning. I can go home, even though I'll be tired too, because this is hard work for both of us, I think and try and identify those parts that will make it easier. Let's do it that way because I know at this time of day, I think both you and I were a little tired yesterday and I'm starting to feel that way now. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is better. But I would like to say something else what is most tiring to me here. Right now, this third time at the Tribunal, I am getting the most tired. Why not? Because I gave several statements to the same circumstances and now I'm afraid, because I'm tired, I might not say exactly the same thing and I don't want it to be -- to seem as if I was not telling the truth or anything like that. But in any case my intentions are not bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that and I believe that's absolutely true. I know you're meticulous and you've expressed several times, not only here but in your prior testimonies and in your interview, that it's important to you not to make a mistake. So I understand that and I don't want to push you into a situation like that. Do you want to go on for another 10 or 15 minutes today or would you like to recess now?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me then go away from that document for now and I'll take you to Exhibit P1615. It's tab number 4. And let me actually skip over that one and go to tab 5, that's more important. Witness, tab 5, Exhibit Number P531. And I'll hand you a hard copy because it's two pages. I'll tell you as that's coming around to you, it's dated the 23rd of March, 1992. We need to get the -- yeah. It's from President Radovan Karadzic to all municipal presidents, I guess SDS presidents. And in paragraph 2, it says: [As read] "Assessing that an important condition for the protection of the Serbian people in the current situation is the rapid and timely transmission of data and information of significance for defence and security, and the passing on of decisions, directives, and instructions from the administrative organs, we have established a Republican Operations Centre and have decided that, besides the district centre in Banja Luka, municipal centres in other areas will assume the role of district centres." I think you told me before you had not heard of the republic communications centre or how about this term, the republican operations centre --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly ask that the witness repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I talked over you. The interpreters ask if you can repeat your last answer.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard of it. I'm looking at this paper and seeing this for the first time. This is the first time that I'm hearing about this operations centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If you would go down two more paragraphs it says: [As read] "The district centres in Banja Luka, Trebinje, Sokolac, and Bijeljina are already linked with the Republican TT, telephone and telegraph centre, and by radio link, while the district centres in Sekovici and Petrovo will be connected by 26 March 1992." Did you know about this communications system in March of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you another document that may relate. This is tab 69 in Exhibit P1725. I think you can work off the screen on this one. It will be up in a minute and you should see it's dated the 18th of June, 1992, from Minister of Defence Colonel Bogdan Subotic. It's addressed to the ministries of the government advising them that: [As read] "The communications centre at Pale can send telegrams to the Serbian Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina and to other Serbian autonomous regions, which can be used for notifications and requests." Did you know about that communications system which apparently was associated with the government or with the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it's not defined here what communications centre? Communications centre is the official name and it's known who that refers to, the communications centre of the Ministry of the Interior and this is some communications centre at Pale. This is an amateur thing. Which communications centre? I never heard of a communications centre in Pale through which us communications personnel were supposed to -- I don't know, what sort of a communications centre in Pale? This was municipal, military, police type of centre? I don't know what it refers to. We had nothing to do with it. I said at the time that they -- my operators had some phone number which if they managed to get through, they did; if not -- this was a number to Pale. So sometimes it would succeed and sometimes not. It did not matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You talked about --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: There is one mistake in the transcript. 77, line -- paragraph -- no -- page 77 and line 2 and 3. Because what was recorded was it was said -- 5 and 6. "This was military, police type of centre," but that's not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, did you hear that. The transcript says: [As read] "I don't know what sort of a communications centre in Pale? This was military, police type of centre." Is that what you said or did you say something different?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I said the first line right away after the heading it says the communications centre in Pale is possible. Everything else to me makes no sense. If you don't know who it is, then I don't care what. You know, communications centre, communications centre of what? Military? Police? The ham radio operators? We had ham radio operators during the war. I don't know. So for me, that means nothing. Had I received that then -- I am seeing this paper now for the first time and I have nothing to say now other than what I have already said. If there is no name, then it's nothing, that communications centre has no name, communications centre in Pale. Only God knows what could have been in Pale. Said the MUP communications centre, the CJB communications centre, the communications centre of the police in Pale, then I would have known what we had here, but this I have no idea. So it makes no sense to make any further assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take it then that you weren't aware of the provision under the Law on Defence from 1 June 1992 in the Republika Srpska provided that the Ministry of Defence was to establish communications for the purposes of command and control in the case of war or imminent threat of war. Did you know about -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know a Mr. Vukovic who worked in the republican centre for that body that you described in Prijedor that dealt with the early warning system for disasters and floods and sounding the air-raid siren, that kind of thing? Did you know that there was a central office for that organisation in Pale?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know. It's possible that it was there and possibly it was not -- I did not convey any information to them. I don't know. I don't know Vukovic. There are a number of Vukovic's. The only Vukovic I knew was an engineer who worked in Banja Luka in the state security before the war -- security, Vukovic, Drago, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, different guy. What about -- did you know a Nebojsa Savic who had some dealings in working with communications?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew something. He was a ham radio operator. Before the war he worked in the SUP of Sarajevo. He was a policeman before, then he joined communications, I don't know when, then he was this guy who writes the dispatches like those guys of mine, Sarac and others. And then shortly before the war he went into the maintenance and repair of radio equipment. And all of that was as part of the Sarajevo city SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You weren't aware of any work he did in setting up a clandestine communications system for the SDS before the start of the war in 1992? Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war? No, I don't know what he could have done. He was a ham radio operator, that's true. But I don't know what he was doing in Sarajevo. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In Prijedor after the 30th of April, 1992, during 1992 did you ever have any occasion to try to communicate directly with MUP headquarters, whether it was in Pale or somewhere else in Sarajevo or in Bijeljina? Did you have any direct communication with them in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave the example earlier of that director, the Laki [phoen] award recipient. I didn't really talk about that. After the 30th of April, a large number appeared in schools and all over the place of those who wanted to be directors. For example, a Muslim was a director before so others wanted to be directors. And so one of them addressed me, I didn't know him before, his name was Milenko Vracar, I think, if he could send a fax to Pale to the ministry, their Ministry of Education, so that they would agree that he could be a director. He was brought by some guy from the SDS Dusko -- I don't know what his name was. Well, it doesn't matter. I knew the person from security who had brought him. And knowing that these communications were not really going well, not operating, and I said: Well, there's no chance. But then I thought I don't want to refuse you so just leave that paper and we will send it. And can you imagine, he had the luck and in about two or three minutes there was approval for him -- that came back for him to be a minister -- no, I mean, not a minister -- I mean, it was like winning the lottery as far as I was concerned. So judging by his example, we concluded that the communications were really working. Sometimes it would take a few days for something to get through to Pale, but in his case it was very quick. So the communications went through very poorly, but then again you have this factor of probability. Some important things did not get through and something that was not important did. And there you have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know it's five minutes early, but I think this would be a good place for me to break, organise myself and try and finish everything else in one session tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we resume at 9.00 tomorrow in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 14th day of October, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.38 p.m.,
